project.name: supertonic
project.description: Supertonic is a lightning-fast, on-device multilingual text-to-speech SDK that runs entirely locally via ONNX Runtime, with no cloud calls; this repository collects ready-to-use ONNX Runtime usage examples for the Supertonic TTS model across 11 language/platform targets (Python, Node.js, browser via Vite/WebGPU, Java, C++, C#, Go, Swift/iOS, Rust, and Flutter).

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the top-level README to understand what Supertonic is: a lightning-fast, on-device, 99M-parameter multilingual TTS model that runs entirely via ONNX Runtime — no cloud, no API calls. The README frames the rest of the repo: the Python SDK (pip install supertonic) is the canonical reference, and every other folder is a hand-written ONNX Runtime example showing how to reconstruct the same synthesis pipeline in another language. Skim the quick-start examples to see how identical the API looks across Python, Node.js, Browser, Java, C++, C#, Go, Swift, iOS, Rust, and Flutter.

tour.title: Python: The Canonical Pipeline (helper.py)
tour.description: Open the Python helper module — this is the reference implementation that every other language port mirrors. It defines the three core building blocks: UnicodeProcessor (NFKD text normalization + per-language tagging), Style (loads voice-style JSONs that condition the model), and TextToSpeech (loads four ONNX sessions — duration predictor, text encoder, vector estimator, vocoder — and orchestrates the iterative diffusion-style inference loop that turns text into 44.1 kHz audio). Read this once and you will recognize the same four-stage pipeline in cpp/helper.cpp, rust/helper.rs, swift/Helper.swift, and every other port.
tour.languageLesson: Python's ONNX Runtime bindings (`onnxruntime.InferenceSession`) accept NumPy arrays as inputs and return them as outputs — the entire data plane is contiguous float32/int64 arrays. Voice styles ship as JSON blobs of style vectors, which keeps the conditioning data human-inspectable and decoupled from the model weights.

tour.title: Python: CLI Entry Point and PyPI Package
tour.description: Now see how the pipeline is consumed. example_onnx.py is the from-source demo — it parses CLI flags, instantiates TextToSpeech from helper.py, chunks the input text into sentences, runs synthesis, and writes a WAV via soundfile. example_pypi.py shows the alternative: `from supertonic import TTS`, the published package that wraps everything in a one-liner. These two files demonstrate the two ways developers will actually use Supertonic — and every other language folder in the repo follows the same `helper + example_onnx` split.

tour.title: Python: Packaging and Dependencies
tour.description: Look at the Python build manifests to see the minimal dependency surface: onnxruntime, numpy, and soundfile do all the heavy lifting; no PyTorch, no TensorFlow, no cloud SDK. pyproject.toml declares the project metadata and build backend, while requirements.txt pins the runtime dependencies that helper.py actually imports. This minimal footprint — model + runtime + math + audio I/O — is the recipe every other language port reproduces with its native equivalents.

tour.title: Node.js and Browser: JavaScript Ports
tour.description: The two JavaScript targets reuse the same helper/example split with onnxruntime-node (server) and onnxruntime-web (browser, with optional WebGPU acceleration). nodejs/helper.js is a near line-for-line CommonJS port of py/helper.py — UnicodeProcessor, Style, TextToSpeech — driven by example_onnx.js as a CLI script. web/helper.js does the same but runs in a browser; web/main.js wires the pipeline to DOM controls for an interactive demo. Notice how both reuse the canonical four-ONNX-session architecture.
tour.languageLesson: onnxruntime-web ships two backends: WASM (universal, CPU) and WebGPU (modern browsers, GPU-accelerated). Vite's `optimizeDeps.exclude` and `assetsInclude` are used in web/vite.config.js to surface the .wasm and .jsep.wasm worker assets at runtime.

tour.title: C++: Systems Reference Implementation
tour.description: The C++ example is the systems-language reference. helper.h declares the public surface — Config, UnicodeProcessor, Style, TextToSpeech, OnnxModels — and helper.cpp provides the same four-stage pipeline as py/helper.py but using the C++ ONNX Runtime C++ API. example_onnx.cpp is the thin CLI driver. CMakeLists.txt links everything against ONNX Runtime as a shared library and produces a single example_onnx binary. This is what "on-device, zero-overhead inference" looks like at the metal.
tour.languageLesson: ONNX Runtime's C++ API wraps inputs as `Ort::Value` tensors with explicit shape/dtype and uses `Ort::Session::Run` for inference. Linking against the prebuilt onnxruntime shared library keeps the example portable across Linux/macOS without requiring a custom build.

tour.title: Go and Rust: Modern Systems Ports
tour.description: Go and Rust both reach ONNX Runtime through community wrappers — Go uses cgo bindings against the same native libonnxruntime, while Rust uses the `ort` crate. Both ports replicate the canonical pipeline: helper.go / helper.rs implement Config, text preprocessing, voice-style loading, and the multi-session inference loop; example_onnx.go / example_onnx.rs handle CLI parsing (flag in Go, clap in Rust) and WAV writing (hound in Rust). Reading these side-by-side highlights how the same algorithm projects cleanly into each language's idioms.
tour.languageLesson: Rust's `ndarray` crate provides NumPy-equivalent N-dimensional arrays with strict ownership semantics — perfect for ONNX tensors. The `ort` crate accepts `&Array` slices as inputs and returns owned arrays, so the borrow checker enforces tensor lifetimes at compile time.

tour.title: Java and C#: Enterprise Runtime Ports
tour.description: Java and C# bring Supertonic into JVM and .NET environments. Helper.java and Helper.cs each replicate the canonical pipeline using Microsoft's official ONNX Runtime bindings (com.microsoft.onnxruntime / Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime — both maintained by the same team). The ExampleONNX entry points expose the same CLI flag surface as their Python sibling. pom.xml (Maven) and Supertonic.csproj (.NET SDK-style) declare the ONNX Runtime dependencies and the main-class wiring needed to invoke the demos.
tour.languageLesson: Both Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime (NuGet) and com.microsoft.onnxruntime (Maven Central) wrap the same native runtime as the C++ example. Tensors are constructed from primitive arrays plus shape metadata — Java uses OnnxTensor.createTensor, .NET uses OrtValue.CreateTensorValueFromMemory.

tour.title: Swift CLI: SwiftPM Port
tour.description: The Swift folder is the command-line port — a Swift Package Manager executable that runs on macOS and Linux. Package.swift declares a single ExampleONNX target depending on onnxruntime-swift-package-manager. Helper.swift is the canonical pipeline in Swift idioms (structs for Config, the Unicode preprocessor, the chunker, and the TextToSpeech driver coordinating four ONNX sessions); Sources/ExampleONNX.swift is the CLI driver. This is distinct from the SwiftUI iOS app you will see next — same language, different deployment target.

tour.title: iOS App: SwiftUI Mobile Demo
tour.description: The iOS example demonstrates the same pipeline embedded in a real mobile app. App.swift is the SwiftUI @main entry; ContentView.swift renders the demo UI (text input, language picker, NFE slider, play button); TTSViewModel.swift is a MainActor ObservableObject binding @Published state to the view; TTSService.swift is the async wrapper that loads the bundled ONNX models and exposes synthesize(). Unlike the Swift CLI, here the ONNX assets are bundled into the .app via project.yml (XcodeGen) so the model ships inside the binary — true on-device inference with zero network calls.
tour.languageLesson: SwiftUI's @MainActor + @Published pattern keeps UI updates thread-safe while heavy ONNX inference runs off-main via `async`. The XcodeGen project.yml replaces a hand-edited .xcodeproj with a declarative spec, making the iOS demo reproducible without committing Xcode's binary project files.

tour.title: Flutter: Cross-Platform Mobile Port
tour.description: The Flutter example is the multi-platform Dart port. lib/helper.dart re-implements the canonical four-stage TTS pipeline using flutter_onnxruntime, including the NFKD text decomposition and the iterative denoising loop. lib/main.dart bootstraps a Material UI with controls for text, denoising steps, speed, and language, then plays the synthesized audio through just_audio. pubspec.yaml declares dependencies and crucially bundles the ONNX models and voice_styles JSONs as Flutter assets — the same on-device-inference story as iOS, but cross-platform.

tour.title: Cross-Language Test Harness
tour.description: Finally, see how all 11 language targets are exercised together. test_all.sh is the top-level harness that walks each language folder, builds the example (cmake/cargo/maven/npm/pip/etc.), runs example_onnx with a canonical prompt, captures timings, and aggregates pass/fail statistics. This is the closest thing the repo has to CI: it proves that every language port really does produce equivalent WAV output from the same input text. It is also the best place to look when you need a working build/run incantation for any language target.
tour.languageLesson: A POSIX shell harness like test_all.sh keeps multi-language CI portable without depending on GitHub Actions YAML or any platform-specific orchestrator — anyone with bash and the per-language toolchains installed can reproduce the full test matrix locally.
